title: Sarampión: de la eliminación al rebrote. Revisión de la literatura y recomendaciones actuales
abstract: El sarampión es una enfermedad viral altamente contagiosa, prevenible por vacunación y de notificación obligatoria, que representa un problema de salud pública vigente. Su agente causal es el virus del sarampión (familia Paramyxoviridae), de serotipo único, transmitido por vía aérea con un número reproductivo básico de 12 a 18. La presentación clínica clásica incluye un pródromo de fiebre, tos, coriza y conjuntivitis, seguido de las manchas de Koplik y un exantema maculopapular cefalocaudal. El diagnóstico se confirma mediante serología (IgM específica), reacción en cadena de la polimerasa o cultivo viral. El tratamiento es fundamentalmente de soporte; en pacientes pediátricos, la vitamina A reduce la mortalidad hasta un 62%, por lo que está recomendada por la OMS en este grupo de pacientes. Las complicaciones ocurren en aproximadamente el 30% de los casos; las más frecuentes son diarrea (8%) y otitis media (7-9%), y las complicaciones graves incluyen neumonía, diarrea, encefalitis aguda, encefalomielitis aguda posinfecciosa y, a largo plazo, panencefalitis esclerosante subaguda. Las poblaciones más vulnerables son los menores de 5 años, los adultos jóvenes sin inmunización previa, las embarazadas y los inmunocomprometidos. La vacuna triple vírica (sarampión, rubeola y parotiditis) tiene una eficacia del 97% tras dos dosis y requiere una cobertura poblacional superior al 93% para alcanzar la inmunidad de rebaño. En México, la cobertura vacunal ha disminuido significativamente, lo que derivó en más de 12,000 casos confirmados y más de 33 defunciones durante el brote de 2025-2026, afectando mayoritariamente a niños no vacunados. La profilaxis posexposición con la vacuna triple vírica en un plazo de 72 horas, o con inmunoglobulina en un plazo de 6 días, está indicada para personas susceptibles de alto riesgo. La coordinación mundial, las campañas de vacunación sostenidas y una mayor vigilancia clínica siguen siendo fundamentales para frenar la transmisión.

analysis.summary_en: This study addresses the ongoing public health problem of measles, emphasizing its high contagiousness, prevention through vaccination, and the need for continuous surveillance. The research highlights the clinical presentation of measles, including the characteristic prodrome and rash, and outlines diagnostic methods such as serology, PCR, and viral culture. It also discusses the importance of supportive treatment, particularly the role of vitamin A in reducing mortality among pediatric patients. The study notes that complications occur in about 30% of cases, with common issues like diarrhea and otitis media and severe outcomes such as pneumonia and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Vulnerable populations include children under five, unvaccinated adults, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals. The paper underscores the critical role of vaccination coverage, with the triple viral vaccine showing 97% efficacy after two doses and requiring over 93% population coverage for herd immunity. It also references the significant decline in vaccination coverage in Mexico, leading to over 12,000 confirmed cases and more than 33 deaths during the 2025-2026 outbreak, primarily affecting unvaccinated children. The study concludes that global coordination, sustained vaccination campaigns, and enhanced clinical vigilance remain essential to control transmission.

title: Comparative Performance of CNN and HOG-LBP-Based SVM for Mpox Classification
abstract: Skin lesions caused by mpox may visually resemble those resulting from other skin diseases, making image-based classification a potential approach to support preliminary screening. This study aimed to compare the performance of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and a Support Vector Machine (SVM) using combined Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) and Local Binary Patterns (LBP) features for binary classification of mpox and other skin lesion images. The experimental dataset consisted of 224 unique original images, comprising 116 mpox images and 108 images of other conditions, including chickenpox and measles. The SVM employed a 23,250-dimensional HOG-LBP feature vector with a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel, whereas the CNN automatically learned visual representations from preprocessed RGB images. Both models were evaluated using identical stratified five-fold cross-validation partitions, with data splitting performed before augmentation and hyperparameter tuning conducted within the training partitions. Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and specificity. The CNN achieved an average accuracy of 84.37%, precision of 88.73%, recall of 80.25%, F1-score of 84.06%, and specificity of 88.92%. Meanwhile, the SVM achieved 83.03%, 84.87%, 81.92%, 83.32%, and 84.28%, respectively. The results indicate that the CNN achieved higher performance in four evaluation metrics, while the SVM obtained slightly higher recall. These findings demonstrate that both approaches offer different classification strengths within the evaluated dataset. Nevertheless, further evaluation using independent datasets and more diverse skin lesion images is necessary to assess their generalizability before potential application in preliminary mpox screening.

title_zh: CNN 和基于 HOG-LBP 的 SVM 在 Mpox 分类中的性能比较
source_body_en: Skin lesions caused by mpox may visually resemble those resulting from other skin diseases, making image-based classification a potential approach to support preliminary screening. This study aimed to compare the performance of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and a Support Vector Machine (SVM) using combined Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) and Local Binary Patterns (LBP) features for binary classification of mpox and other skin lesion images. The experimental dataset consisted of 224 unique original images, comprising 116 mpox images and 108 images of other conditions, including chickenpox and measles. The SVM employed a 23,250-dimensional HOG-LBP feature vector with a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel, whereas the CNN automatically learned visual representations from preprocessed RGB images. Both models were evaluated using identical stratified five-fold cross-validation partitions, with data splitting performed before augmentation and hyperparameter tuning conducted within the training partitions. Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and specificity. The CNN achieved an average accuracy of 84.37%, precision of 88.73%, recall of 80.25%, F1-score of 84.06%, and specificity of 88.92%. Meanwhile, the SVM achieved 83.03%, 84.87%, 81.92%, 83.32%, and 84.28%, respectively. The results indicate that the CNN achieved higher performance in four evaluation metrics, while the SVM obtained slightly higher recall. These findings demonstrate that both approaches offer different classification strengths within the evaluated dataset. Nevertheless, further evaluation using independent datasets and more diverse skin lesion images is necessary to assess their generalizability before potential application in preliminary mpox screening.

title: Perception of Socio-Cultural and Socio-Demographic Determinants ofVaccine-Preventable Disease Occurrence Among Mothers of Under-Five Children in Ilorin West Local Government Area, Kwara State
abstract: Background: This study examined mothers' perceived and self-reported prevalence of vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs), and their perceived socio-cultural and socio-demographic determinants of VPD occurrence, among children under five years in Ilorin West Local Government Area, Kwara State, Nigeria. Methodology: A quantitative descriptive survey design was adopted among mothers of children under five years resident in Ilorin West Local Government Area. A multistage sampling procedure involving stratification, simple random sampling, and systematic random sampling was used to select 418 respondents. A researcher structured questionnaire was used for data collection. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests at 0.05 alpha level. Results: Mothers reported that vaccine-preventable diseases, principally measles (21.3%) and pertussis (16.3%), were perceived as prevalent among their children, with a pooled affirmative response rate of 9.1% across seven disease items. Mothers also held moderately positive socio-cultural beliefs, attitudes and practices favouring immunisation (grand mean = 2.68/4.00), and perceived sociodemographic factors, particularly maternal education, household income, and antenatal care attendance (grand mean = 2.76/4.00), as linked to VPD occurrence. Conclusion: Socio-cultural and socio-demographic factors remain influential, perceived determinants of the vaccine-preventable disease burden in Ilorin West Local Government Area, Kwara State.

The study suggests that these factors are influential in shaping perceptions of vaccine-preventable disease burden. The findings can inform public health strategies to address vaccine hesitancy and improve immunisation rates. However, the reliance on self-reported data introduces potential bias, limiting the strength of the evidence.

title_zh: 夸拉州伊洛林西部地方政府地区五岁以下儿童母亲对疫苗可预防疾病发生的社会文化和社会人口决定因素的看法
source_body_en: Background: This study examined mothers' perceived and self-reported prevalence of vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs), and their perceived socio-cultural and socio-demographic determinants of VPD occurrence, among children under five years in Ilorin West Local Government Area, Kwara State, Nigeria. Methodology: A quantitative descriptive survey design was adopted among mothers of children under five years resident in Ilorin West Local Government Area. A multistage sampling procedure involving stratification, simple random sampling, and systematic random sampling was used to select 418 respondents. A researcher structured questionnaire was used for data collection. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests at 0.05 alpha level. Results: Mothers reported that vaccine-preventable diseases, principally measles (21.3%) and pertussis (16.3%), were perceived as prevalent among their children, with a pooled affirmative response rate of 9.1% across seven disease items. Mothers also held moderately positive socio-cultural beliefs, attitudes and practices favouring immunisation (grand mean = 2.68/4.00), and perceived sociodemographic factors, particularly maternal education, household income, and antenatal care attendance (grand mean = 2.76/4.00), as linked to VPD occurrence. Conclusion: Socio-cultural and socio-demographic factors remain influential, perceived determinants of the vaccine-preventable disease burden in Ilorin West Local Government Area, Kwara State.
abstract_zh: 背景:本研究调查了尼日利亚夸拉州伊洛林西部地方政府区五岁以下儿童中母亲对 疫苗 可预防疾病 (VPD) 的感知和自我报告的 患病率,以及她们感知到的 VPD 发生的社会文化和社会人口决定因素。方法:对伊洛林西部地方政府地区居住的五岁以下儿童的母亲采用了定量描述性调查设计。采用分层、简单随机抽样和系统随机抽样的多阶段抽样程序选择了 418 名受访者。使用研究人员结构化调查问卷来收集数据。使用描述性统计和 0.05 alpha 水平的卡方检验对数据进行分析。结果:母亲们报告,疫苗 可预防疾病,主要是 麻疹 (21.3%) 和百日咳 (16.3%),被认为在她们的孩子中流行,七种疾病项目的汇总肯定反应率为 9.1%。母亲们还持有适度积极的有利于免疫接种的社会文化信仰、态度和做法(总体平均值 = 2.68/4.00),并认为社会人口因素,特别是母亲教育、家庭收入和产前护理就诊率(总体平均值 = 2.76/4.00),与 VPD 的发生有关。结论:社会文化和社会人口因素仍然具有影响力,是夸拉州伊洛林西地方政府地区 疫苗 可预防疾病负担的决定因素。

full_text: Article summary Vaccine hesitancy poses a significant challenge to achieving optimal immunization coverage, particularly in regions like Nigeria where measles remains a public health threat. This study identified key determinants of measles vaccine hesitancy among caregivers in Ogun State, revealing that younger caregiver age, cultural or religious beliefs, and logistical barriers such as vaccine availability and travel time to facilities significantly influence hesitancy levels. Abstract Background Measles remains a major public health concern in Nigeria despite the availability of effective vaccines. Vaccine hesitancy among caregivers threatens the achievement of optimal immunization coverage this study assessed the determinants of measles vaccine hesitancy among caregivers of under-five children in Ado-Odo/Ota and Odeda Local Government Areas of Ogun State. Methods A mixed-methods cross-sectional study was conducted among 368 caregivers selected using a multistage sampling technique. Quantitative data were collected using structured questionnaires and analyzed using IBM SPSS version 27. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and logistic regression were used to determine associations and predictors of vaccine hesitancy. Qualitative data were collected through six focus group discussions with 42 caregivers and analyzed using QualCoder V.3.8.2. Results The prevalence of vaccine hesitancy was 44.6%. At the individual level, age group was significantly associated with vaccine hesitancy (p = 0.028), with younger caregivers more likely to be hesitant. Knowledge (p = 0.774) and attitude (p = 0.442) were not significantly associated with vaccine hesitancy in multivariate analysis. However, qualitative findings revealed substantial gaps in schedule-specific knowledge. At the health system level, vaccine availability (p = 0.031) and time to facility (p = 0.004) were significantly associated with hesitancy. At the community level, cultural and religious influences were significant (p = 0.011). Logistic regression identified younger caregiver age (AOR = 1.91; 95% CI: 1.10–3.32; reference: age 38–49 years), cultural or religious beliefs that discourage vaccination (AOR = 0.52; 95% CI: 0.31–0.86; reference: beliefs that discourage vaccination), travel time of less than 30 min to the vaccination facility (AOR = 0.44; 95% CI: 0.22–0.90; reference: travel time exceeding one hour), and consistent vaccine availability (AOR = 0.63; 95% CI: 0.39–0.99; reference: experience of vaccine stock-outs) as significant predictors. Conclusion Measles vaccine hesitancy is significantly associated with structural, community, and interpersonal factors. Similar content being viewed by others 1 Introduction Vaccine hesitancy has emerged as a major global public health challenge, undermining immunization programmes and contributing to the persistence of vaccine-preventable diseases despite the availability of effective vaccines. It is defined as the delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite the availability of vaccination services and is influenced by complex behavioural and social factors that vary across settings [1, 2]. Recent evidence suggests that vaccine hesitancy remains substantial globally, with prevalence estimates ranging between 25% and 42% across different populations, driven largely by misinformation, declining trust in institutions, and evolving perceptions of vaccine risk [3]. Measles, one of the most contagious vaccine-preventable diseases, continues to pose a significant global health threat, particularly among children under five years of age. Despite the availability of safe and effective vaccines, measles has re-emerged in many regions due to suboptimal immunization coverage. In 2023, over 10 million measles cases were reported globally, reflecting persistent gaps in vaccination coverage below the 95% threshold required for herd immunity [4]. In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), including Nigeria, these gaps are further exacerbated by systemic health challenges and demand-side barriers that limit vaccine uptake [5]. Vaccination decisions are shaped by cultural and religious influences, which vary across settings and can affect caregiver acceptance of childhood vaccines [6]. In addition, vaccine hesitancy has been demonstrated to be a measurable and relevant challenge for childhood immunization, with caregivers’ knowledge, attitudes, and socio-demographic characteristics significantly associated with hesitancy and vaccination behavior [7]. Globally, efforts to control measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases are increasingly undermined by insufficient immunization coverage. In Europe, vaccine hesitancy has emerged as a major barrier to achieving adequate vaccination rates, whereas in regions such as sub-Saharan Africa, coverage challenges often result from a combination of factors including limited access and vaccine availability [8]. In Ethiopia, studies have identified fear of side effects, misconceptions about vaccine safety, and low confidence in immunization services as significant predictors of vaccine hesitancy, with evidence suggesting that effective communication and community engagement can improve trust and correct misinformation [9]. In Nigeria, measles remains a major contributor to childhood morbidity and mortality, with recurrent outbreaks reported across multiple states. National immunization coverage remains suboptimal, and recent surveillance reports indicate thousands of confirmed measles cases annually, reflecting both structural weaknesses and behavioural barriers to vaccination [10, 11]. Ogun State, despite relatively stronger immunization infrastructure compared to other regions, continues to experience recurring measles cases, suggesting that factors beyond vaccine availability contribute to persistent immunity gaps. Nigeria’s linguistic and cultural diversity presents challenges for vaccination promotion, particularly among rural and less-educated populations where access to and comprehension of vaccine information may be limited. Evidence shows that the use of local languages in health education improves caregivers’ knowledge and attitudes toward vaccination [12]. Caregiver decision-making is further influenced by perceptions of vaccine risks and benefits, trust in healthcare providers, religious beliefs, and prevailing social norms, with lower trust and safety concerns commonly associated with vaccine hesitancy [13]. Evidence from LMICs indicates that vaccination uptake is shaped by a combination of demographic, socioeconomic, service-related, and belief-based factors [14]. Health system barriers such as long waiting times, vaccine stockouts, and negative interactions with healthcare workers have been consistently associated with incomplete immunization uptake [15]. In addition, misinformation, distrust in health systems, and community-level narratives have been identified as key drivers of vaccine hesitancy, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa [16]. Cultural and religious beliefs further shape caregivers’ vaccination decisions, with evidence showing that such influences may either promote or hinder vaccine acceptance depending on local context [17]. Vaccine decision-making is therefore influenced by multiple interacting factors operating at individual, interpersonal, community, and health system levels, as conceptualized by the Social Ecological Model [18]. This multilevel perspective is particularly relevant in settings where vaccines are available but uptake remains suboptimal, highlighting the need to understand how these determinants interact within specific local contexts. Caregiver vaccine hesitancy is influenced by a combination of individual and contextual factors, including limited knowledge, concerns about adverse effects, misinformation, religious beliefs, and constraints related to access and resources. Evidence from systematic reviews and cross-sectional studies consistently identifies lack of reliable vaccine information, fear of side effects, and cultural or faith-based beliefs as key drivers of delayed or refused vaccination across settings [19, 20]. Misinformation and limited access to credible health information further amplify safety concerns, while socioeconomic barriers such as transportation costs and competing priorities compound these effects. Religious and cultural influences remain particularly important, with evidence showing that faith-based beliefs may either promote or hinder vaccine uptake depending on context [21]. Community engagement strategies, including collaboration with trusted religious and traditional leaders, have been shown to effectively address misinformation and improve vaccine uptake [22]. Despite extensive research on vaccine hesitancy globally and nationally, there remains limited localized evidence examining how these multi-level determinants operate within specific communities in Ogun State. Ado-Odo/Ota and Odeda LGAs differ in terms of urbanization, access to health services, and sociocultural dynamics, yet empirical data on vaccine hesitancy within these areas remain scarce. This study therefore assessed the determinants of measles vaccine hesitancy among caregivers of under-five children in Ado-Odo/Ota and Odeda LGAs of Ogun State using a mixed-methods approach. 2 Conceptual framework The Social Ecological Model (SEM) guided the selection and interpretation of study variables. Individual-level factors included caregivers’ age, educational status, knowledge, and attitudes towards measles vaccination. Interpersonal factors comprised social, cultural, and religious influences on vaccination decisions. Community-level factors were explored through focus group discussions and included prevailing community beliefs and norms regarding childhood vaccination. Health-system factors included vaccine availability and accessibility of vaccination services, such as travel time to health facilities. The SEM was further used to organize and integrate the quantitative and qualitative findings. 3 Methods 3.1 Study design A mixed-methods cross-sectional study design was employed to assess the determinants of measles vaccine hesitancy among caregivers of under-five children. The quantitative component utilized a descriptive cross-sectional approach to examine associations between socio-demographic, healthcare service-related, and psychosocial factors and vaccine hesitancy. The qualitative component complemented these findings by exploring caregivers’ experiences, beliefs, and contextual influences through focus group discussions (FGDs), enabling triangulation of results. To reflect this design, the Methods section is organized into two subsections: the Quantitative Survey and the Qualitative Interviews. 3.2 Study setting The study was conducted in Ado-Odo/Ota and Odeda Local Government Areas (LGAs) of Ogun State, Nigeria. Ogun State is located in the South-West geopolitical zone of Nigeria and shares boundaries with Lagos, Oyo, and Ondo States. Ado-Odo/Ota is predominantly urban and industrial, whereas Odeda is semi-urban with significant rural settlements. These LGAs were purposively selected due to their contrasting socio-demographic characteristics and documented occurrence of measles cases between 2022 and 2024. While Ado-Odo/Ota is densely populated with diverse populations, Odeda has experienced recurrent outbreaks despite immunization efforts. Findings from this study are therefore context specific. 3.3 Quantitative survey 3.3.1 Study population The study population comprised caregivers (mothers, fathers, and guardians) of children aged 0–59 months residing in the selected LGAs. 3.3.2 Eligibility criteria Caregivers who had resided in the study areas for at least six months, had children aged 0–59 months, and provided informed consent were included. Caregivers who were not directly responsible for immunization decisions or declined participation were excluded. 3.3.3 Sample size determination The sample size was determined using the Cochran formula for single proportions: Where: n = minimum sample size, Z = standard normal deviate at 95% confidence level (1.96), p = estimated prevalence of vaccine hesitancy (0.32), d = margin of error (0.05). The minimum sample size was determined using Cochran formula and based on a vaccine hesitancy prevalence of 32% [23]. Substituting these values yielded a minimum sample size of 334. After adjusting for a 10% non-response rate, the final sample size was 368 participants. Due to the multistage sampling design, proportional allocation was applied across selected LGAs and wards to ensure representativeness of the study population. A design effect was not applied in the sample size calculation. This was because the intra-cluster correlation coefficient (ICC) for vaccine hesitancy was unknown in this setting, and published ICC estimates for immunization outcomes in similar Nigerian contexts were not available. Post-hoc sensitivity analysis indicated that the achieved sample size of 368 would still provide adequate power (≥ 80%) to detect an odds ratio of 1.5 or greater for key predictors, assuming a design effect of up to 2.0. This is acknowledged as a limitation of the study. 3.3.4 Sampling technique and procedure A multistage sampling technique was employed in selecting study participants. Stage 1 Ado-Odo/Ota LGA (16 wards) and Odeda LGA (10 wards) were included in the study. To ensure representativeness, 50% of wards were selected from each LGA using simple random sampling by balloting. Accordingly, eight wards were selected from Ado-Odo/Ota LGA and five wards from Odeda LGA. Following sample size determination, proportionate allocation was used to distribute the study sample across the two LGAs based on their estimated populations of under-five children (Table 1). The number of respondents allocated to each LGA and ward was determined by dividing the estimated under-five population of the LGA or ward by the total under-five population of the study area and multiplying by the total sample size. The allocated sample was subsequently distributed proportionately among the selected wards using ward-level estimates of the under-five population (Tables 2 and 3). This ensured that wards with larger under-five populations contributed proportionately more respondents to the study. Stage 2 Within each selected ward, communities were selected using simple random sampling. In some wards, more than one community was selected to ensure that the allocated sample size for that ward was achieved. Overall, in some wards, more than one community was selected to ensure that the allocated sample size was achieved, depending on population size and distribution of eligible households. Stage 3 A household listing was conducted in selected communities. Households were selected using systematic sampling. A random starting point was selected within each community, after which every second household was visited until the allocated sample size for each area was achieved. This approach was adopted due to the absence of a complete household sampling frame in the study areas. Stage 4 One eligible caregiver of a child under five years was selected per household. In households with more than one eligible caregiver, simple random selection was used. Where two eligible caregivers were present, selection was done by tossing a coin, while balloting was used where more than two eligible caregivers were present. No non-response was recorded among eligible caregivers approached, and the final analytic sample comprised 368 caregivers. 3.3.5 Data collection Quantitative data were collected using a structured interviewer-administered questionnaire developed by the authors based on a review of relevant literature on vaccine hesitancy. The questionnaire included items assessing caregivers’ knowledge, attitudes, healthcare service-related factors, and socio-cultural influences on vaccination. 3.3.6 Validity and reliability The instrument was pretested among caregivers in a non-selected LGA. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha, yielding a coefficient of 0.78. Face and content validity were ensured through expert review by public health professionals. 3.3.7 Data analysis Quantitative data were analyzed using IBM SPSS version 27. Descriptive statistics were summarized using frequencies and percentages. Associations between variables were assessed using chi-square tests, while binary logistic regression was performed to identify predictors of vaccine hesitancy. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. There were no missing data in the final analytic dataset, as all 368 completed questionnaires were fully answered. In the event of item non-response during data collection, field supervisors revisited the respondent to obtain complete information. The analysis did not adjust for clustering at the ward or community level, which may lead to underestimated standard errors. 3.3.8 Operationalization of vaccine hesitancy Vaccine hesitancy was operationalized using two items adapted from the WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) Working Group on Vaccine Hesitancy definition: “delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite availability of vaccination services” [2]. Caregivers were asked: (1) “Have you ever delayed your child’s measles vaccination?” and (2) “Have you ever refused a measles vaccine for your child?” Response options were Yes/No. A caregiver was classified as vaccine hesitant if they responded “Yes” to either question, indicating behavioral delay or refusal. Caregivers who responded “No” to both were classified as not hesitant. A binary vaccine hesitancy variable was then created, where caregivers who reported either refusing or delaying a measles vaccine were classified as vaccine hesitant (coded as 1), while those who reported neither behaviour were classified as non-hesitant (coded as 0). This study identified key determinants of measles vaccine hesitancy among caregivers in Ogun State, revealing that younger caregiver age, cultural or religious beliefs, and logistical barriers such as vaccine availability and travel time to facilities significantly influence hesitancy levels. Abstract Background Measles remains a major public health concern in Nigeria despite the availability of effective vaccines. Vaccine hesitancy among caregivers threatens the achievement of optimal immunization coverage this study assessed the determinants of measles vaccine hesitancy among caregivers of under-five children in Ado-Odo/Ota and Odeda Local Government Areas of Ogun State. Methods A mixed-methods cross-sectional study was conducted among 368 caregivers selected using a multistage sampling technique. Quantitative data were collected using structured questionnaires and analyzed using IBM SPSS version 27. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and logistic regression were used to determine associations and predictors of vaccine hesitancy. Qualitative data were collected through six focus group discussions with 42 caregivers and analyzed using QualCoder V.3.8.2. Results The prevalence of vaccine hesitancy was 44.6%. At the individual level, age group was significantly associated with vaccine hesitancy (p = 0.028), with younger caregivers more likely to be hesitant. Knowledge (p = 0.774) and attitude (p = 0.442) were not significantly associated with vaccine hesitancy in multivariate analysis. However, qualitative findings revealed substantial gaps in schedule-specific knowledge. At the health system level, vaccine availability (p = 0.031) and time to facility (p = 0.004) were significantly associated with hesitancy. At the community level, cultural and religious influences were significant (p = 0.011). Logistic regression identified younger caregiver age (AOR = 1.91; 95% CI: 1.10–3.32; reference: age 38–49 years), cultural or religious beliefs that discourage vaccination (AOR = 0.52; 95% CI: 0.31–0.86; reference: beliefs that discourage vaccination), travel time of less than 30 min to the vaccination facility (AOR = 0.44; 95% CI: 0.22–0.90; reference: travel time exceeding one hour), and consistent vaccine availability (AOR = 0.63; 95% CI: 0.39–0.99; reference: experience of vaccine stock-outs) as significant predictors. Conclusion Measles vaccine hesitancy is significantly associated with structural, community, and interpersonal factors. analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在确定尼日利亚奥gun州5岁以下儿童看护者对麻疹 疫苗犹豫不决的决定因素,因为疫苗犹豫不决已成为全球主要的公共卫生挑战,削弱了疫苗接种计划,并导致尽管有有效的疫苗,疫苗可预防疾病仍持续存在。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 采用混合方法的横断面研究,通过多阶段抽样技术选取了368名看护者作为研究对象。研究对象为居住在研究区域至少六个月、且0-59个月儿童的看护者,并已签署知情同意书。
analysis_zh.methods: 定量数据通过结构化问卷收集,并使用IBM SPSS版本27进行分析。采用描述性统计、卡方检验和逻辑回归分析来确定疫苗犹豫不决的相关因素和预测因素。通过Cronbach’s alpha评估内部一致性,得到系数为0.78。
analysis_zh.main_results: 患病率显示疫苗犹豫不决的比例为44.6%。年龄组与疫苗犹豫不决显著相关(p = 0.028),年轻看护者更可能表现出犹豫不决。然而,在多变量分析中,知识(p = 0.774)和态度(p = 0.442)与疫苗犹豫不决无显著关联。定性研究结果揭示了在特定接种时间安排方面的知识显著缺失。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将研究结果解释为表明麻疹 疫苗犹豫不决与结构性、社区性和人际因素显著相关。本研究证明了疫苗犹豫不决是儿童疫苗接种的一个可衡量且相关的重要挑战,看护者的知识、态度和社会人口学特征与犹豫不决和疫苗接种行为显著相关。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为针对结构性、社区性和人际因素的干预措施提供信息,以解决麻疹 疫苗犹豫不决问题,特别是在免疫接种基础设施相对健全但免疫缺口仍然存在的地区。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究具有特定的背景,样本量为368,即使考虑到设计效应高达2.0,仍能提供足够的统计功效(≥ 80%)以检测关键预测因素的比值比为1.5或更高的情况。然而,本研究并未考虑所有潜在的混杂因素。

full_text: Alexandro Bonifaz, Departamento de Dermatología y Micología, Hospital General de México Dr. Eduardo Liceaga, Ciudad de México, México Jesica Naanous-Rayek, Departamento de Dermatología y Micología, Hospital General de México Dr. Eduardo Liceaga, Ciudad de México, México Ana P. Landeta-Sa, Departamento de Dermatología y Micología, Hospital General de México Dr. Eduardo Liceaga, Ciudad de México, México Ana C. Carbajal-César, Departamento de Pediatría y Epidemiología Clínica, Instituto Nacional de Pediatría, Ciudad de México, México Alejandra M. Caused by the measles virus (Paramyxoviridae family), a single-serotype pathogen with a basic reproduction number of 12-18, it is transmitted via aerosolized respiratory droplets. title_original: Measles: from elimination to resurgence. A literature review and current recommendations

analysis.scope_and_question: Measles virus (Morbillivirus hominis), historical taxonomic names, rubeola and measles disease. The review focuses on the epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of measles virus infections, with an emphasis on public health implications and the role of vaccination in controlling outbreaks.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is based on a comprehensive analysis of literature, including clinical studies, epidemiological reports, and public health guidelines. It includes evidence from multiple sources, such as WHO recommendations, clinical case studies, and outbreak data. The review does not explicitly report on meta-analysis or pooled estimates but synthesizes findings from various studies to form a coherent overview of measles virus-related topics.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Measles is a highly contagious, vaccine-preventable viral disease caused by the measles virus, with a basic reproduction number of 12-18. It is transmitted via aerosolized respiratory droplets and presents with a characteristic prodrome followed by a maculopapular rash. Vitamin A supplementation is universally recommended for all diagnosed children, reducing childhood mortality by up to 62%. The MMR vaccine achieves 97% efficacy after two doses and requires population coverage above 93% to sustain herd immunity. Complications occur in approximately 30% of cases, with severe outcomes including pneumonia, acute encephalitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights the importance of maintaining high vaccination rates to prevent outbreaks, but it does not provide specific data on the effectiveness of different vaccination strategies in diverse populations. There is also a lack of detailed information on the long-term effects of measles virus infections and the potential for resurgence in regions with low vaccination coverage. Additionally, the review does not address the role of specific measles virus genotypes in disease severity or transmission dynamics.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Global coordination, sustained vaccination campaigns, and heightened clinical awareness are essential to curb measles transmission. Research should focus on improving vaccination strategies, particularly in vulnerable populations such as children under 5, young adults without prior immunization, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals. Surveillance and diagnostic methods should be enhanced to ensure timely identification and management of measles cases. Post-exposure prophylaxis with MMR vaccine within 72 hours or immunoglobulin within 6 days is recommended for high-risk individuals.

analysis.summary_en: This review provides an overview of measles virus, emphasizing its epidemiology, clinical presentation, and public health significance. It highlights the importance of vaccination in preventing outbreaks and reducing mortality, particularly through vitamin A supplementation. The review underscores the need for global coordination and sustained vaccination efforts to maintain herd immunity. However, it notes gaps in understanding the long-term effects of measles infections and the role of specific genotypes in disease outcomes. Research and practice implications include improving vaccination strategies, enhancing surveillance, and ensuring timely post-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk groups.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 麻疹病毒(人麻疹病毒),历史分类学名称,风疹和 麻疹 疾病。该综述的重点是 流行病学、临床表现、诊断、治疗 和 麻疹病毒 感染的预防,重点是公共卫生影响和 疫苗接种 在控制 暴发 中的作用。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该审查基于对文献的综合分析,包括临床研究、流行病学报告和公共卫生指南。它包括来自多个来源的证据,例如 WHO 建议、临床案例研究和 暴发 数据。该综述没有明确报告荟萃分析或汇总估计,而是综合了各种研究的结果,以形成 麻疹病毒 相关主题的连贯概述。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 麻疹 是一种由 麻疹病毒 引起的高度传染性、疫苗 可预防的病毒性疾病,基本繁殖数为 12-18。它通过雾化呼吸道飞沫传播,并出现典型的前驱症状,随后出现斑丘疹。普遍建议所有确诊儿童补充维生素 A,使儿童 死亡率 减少高达 62%。MMR 疫苗 在两次接种后达到 97% 的功效,并需要 93% 以上的人群覆盖率才能维持群体免疫。大约 30% 的病例会出现并发症,严重后果包括肺炎、急性脑炎和 亚急性硬化性全脑炎。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该综述强调了维持高 疫苗接种 率对于预防 疫苗接种 的重要性,但它没有提供不同 疫苗接种 策略在不同人群中有效性的具体数据。还缺乏关于 麻疹病毒 感染的长期影响以及在 麻疹病毒 覆盖率低的地区重新流行的可能性的详细信息。此外,该综述没有讨论特定 麻疹病毒 基因型在疾病严重程度或 传播 动态中的作用。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 全球协调、持续的 疫苗接种 活动以及提高临床意识对于遏制 麻疹 传播 至关重要。研究应侧重于改进 疫苗接种 策略,特别是针对 5 岁以下儿童、未事先免疫的年轻人、孕妇和免疫功能低下个体等弱势群体。应加强麻疹和诊断方法,确保及时识别和管理麻疹病例。建议高危个体在 72 小时内使用 MMR 疫苗 或在 6 天内使用免疫球蛋白进行暴露后预防。

analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 全球协调、持续的 疫苗接种 活动以及提高临床意识对于遏制 麻疹 传播 至关重要。研究应侧重于改进 疫苗接种 策略,特别是针对 5 岁以下儿童、未事先免疫的年轻人、孕妇和免疫功能低下个体等弱势群体。应加强麻疹和诊断方法,确保及时识别和管理麻疹病例。建议高危个体在 72 小时内使用 MMR 疫苗 或在 6 天内使用免疫球蛋白进行暴露后预防。

full_text: 269 Measles is an acute infectious disease caused by measles virus infection, the main symptoms being fever, rash, and catarrhal symptoms. The measles virus is extremely contagious. Measles can be transmitted not only by droplet or contact infection but also by airborne transmission. As the measles virus also infects immune cells, it suppresses the immune system of infected individuals and causes various complications. Complications in the respiratory tract (pneumonia, laryngotracheobronchitis) and gastrointestinal tract (diarrhea, stomatitis), as well as otitis media, are frequent. Neurological complications are less common but often more severe, and include measles encephalitis, which appears within about two weeks of infection (approximately 1 case per 1,000 measles cases), and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), which has a poor prognosis and appears several years to more than a decade after infection and recovery (approximately 1 case per tens of thousands of measles cases). The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that an estimated 95,000 persons died from measles in 2024, with the majority being children under five years of age (https:// www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/measles). On the other hand, WHO considers measles to be an infectious disease that can be eliminated, because a safe and effective vaccine is available, subclinical infections are rare, accurate diagnostic methods are available, and humans are the only natural host; thus, WHO aims to eliminate measles. In 2005, the Regional Committee of the WHO Western Pacific Region (WPR), to which Japan belongs, resolved to eliminate measles from the WPR by 2012. In response to this, Japan introduced a two-dose measles-containing vaccine vaccination schedule (1st dose stage and 2nd dose stage) in 2006. Furthermore, in December 2007, the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) issued the “Guidelines on Prevention of Specified Infectious Diseases: Measles” (latest revision in April 2019, hereinafter referred to as the “Guidelines”), and to strengthen the immunity of teenagers, who were the primary demographic affected in domestic outbreaks at the time, measures to eliminate measles were strengthened, including the implementation of a five-year (fiscal years [FY] 2008–2012) supplementary vaccination program for those of an age equivalent to the first year of junior high school (3rd round) and third year of senior high school (4th round) as routine vaccination under the Immunization Act. These measures led to a substantial decrease in measles cases in Japan from 2009, and in 2015, Japan was verified as having eliminated measles by the Regional Verification Commission for Measles Elimination in the WPR. Maintenance of elimination status has been verified through 2024, and documents to be submitted to the Commission regarding the status in 2025 are currently being compiled. Measles notification under the National Epidemiological Surveillance of Infectious Diseases: Measles is a Category V Infectious Disease under the Infectious Diseases Control Law (for notification criteria and disease classification, see https://www.mhlw.go.jp/ bunya/kenkou/kekkaku-kansenshou11/01-05-14-03. html). In 2008, when measles became a notifiable disease, there were 11,013 cases notified. Thereafter, the annual number of notified cases ranged from 35 to 744 through 2019, while the annual number was 10 or fewer during 2020–2022, when various measures, including travel restrictions, were implemented in response to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. Following the complete lifting of border control measures for COVID-19 in 2023, the annual number of notified cases increased to 28 in 2023 and 45 in 2024, and increased substantially to 265 in 2025 (Fig. 1). In terms of disease classification for the 265 case- patients reported in 2025, 62 of the 265 were modified measles, which are atypical laboratory-confirmed cases with only one or two of the three main symptoms (fever, rash, and catarrhal symptoms). Regarding age distribution, patients aged 20 years or older accounted for at least 60% of cases, with particularly large numbers of cases among those in their 20s and 30s (Fig. 2). As for vaccination history, 77 cases had no vaccination, 46 had received one dose, 52 had received two doses, and the vaccination history was unknown for 90 cases; 23 cases were aged less than 1 year and had not yet reached the age for routine vaccination (Table 1). It should be noted that, because the number of unvaccinated persons in the population is considered to be small, caution is required when comparing the number of cases among vaccinated and unvaccinated persons. Detection of measles virus (Infectious Agents Surveillance System): Among the 194 cases in which viral genes were detected at PHIs in 2025 and reported to the Infectious Agents Surveillance System of the National Epidemiological Surveillance of Infectious Diseases system, the viral genotype was B3 in 163 cases and D8 in 23 cases, while in 8 cases viral genes were detected but the nucleotide sequence could not be determined (Table 2). Among the 194 cases, 66 had a history of overseas travel and were suspected to have been infected overseas, while domestic infection was suspected in at least 60%. Among cases with a travel history, 51 had a history of travel to Vietnam, accounting for a large proportion (Table 2). Vaccination coverage: Since FY2006, routine measles vaccination has been implemented for children aged 1 year (the 1st dose stage) and for children in the year prior to entering elementary school (the 2nd dose stage). In FY2024, vaccination coverage was 92.7% for the 1st dose stage and 91.0% for the 2nd dose stage, both below the target coverage of 95% (https://www. mhlw.go.jp/bunya/kenkou/kekkaku-kansenshou21/ hashika.html). Also, the vaccination coverage for both the 1st and 2nd dose stages was the lowest in the past 10 years. National Epidemiological Surveillance of Vaccine- Preventable Diseases (NESVPD): In FY2025, measles antibody titers were measured by enzyme immunoassay (EIA) at PHIs in 20 prefectures under the NESVPD. The overall proportion positive for measles EIA antibody titers ≥2 was 96.1%, exceeding the 95% threshold required to prevent an epidemic (Fig. 4). Further measures to be taken: The number of reported measles cases globally, which was approximately 540,000 in 2019, decreased substantially to fewer than 100,000 in both 2020 and 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic. However, it has remained above 100,000 since 2022, with approximately 280,000 cases reported in 2025, and outbreaks continue in many countries. In Japan, where measles elimination status has been achieved, measles occurrence often begins with cases imported from overseas. In 2025, there was a record-high number of approximately 42.68 million inbound visitors to Japan, and, representing an increase of 15.8% from 2024, the number of Japanese outbound travelers reached approximately 14.73 million (https:// statistics.jnto.go.jp/graph/#graph--inbound--travelers- -transition). Such indications of increasing movement of people between Japan and other countries are considered a factor that further increases the risk of measles occurrence. In 2025, there were also many cases for which the presumed place of infection was considered to be within Japan, underscoring the need to establish an environment in which infection does not spread domestically even when measles virus is imported from overseas. In particular, routine vaccination coverage in FY2024 did not reach the target of 95% for either the 1st or 2nd dose stage, and efforts to improve routine vaccination coverage are considered an important challenge. In addition, imported measles may be brought into Japan not only by inbound visitors but also by residents of Japan after traveling to countries where measles is circulating; therefore, measures such as raising awareness among travelers are also important. In recent years, the presumed countries of infection among imported cases have tended to be Southeast Asian countries, including Vietnam, and continued awareness-raising among travelers to these areas remains important. In addition, in 2025, measles resurged in countries that had previously achieved measles elimination, including Canada and the United Kingdom, resulting in revocation of their elimination status; therefore, raising awareness among travelers to these countries with measles resurgence is also important. Furthermore, because more than 500 measles cases have been confirmed in Japan from January through the end of May 2026, it is necessary to further strengthen collaborative approaches, including information sharing among local governments, MHLW, Japan Institute for Health Security (JIHS), and other relevant organizations, in order to monitor the domestic epidemiologic situation and prevent widespread transmission. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the resurgence of measles in Japan following the relaxation of border control measures and to evaluate the impact of vaccination coverage on disease transmission. The background highlights the global decline in measles cases during the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent increase in reported cases since 2022.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed data from the National Epidemiological Surveillance of Infectious Diseases and the National Epidemiological Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in Japan, covering the period from 2008 to 2025. It included 265 measles cases reported in 2025, with a focus on vaccination status, travel history, and disease classification.
analysis.methods: The study utilized real-time RT-PCR testing for measles virus detection and genotyping of the N gene for viral identification. Measles antibody titers were measured using enzyme immunoassay (EIA) in 20 prefectures under the National Epidemiological Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases.
analysis.main_results: In 2025, 265 measles cases were reported, with 194 cases having detectable viral genes and 186 cases having a determined genotype. analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the high proportion of antibody titers ≥2 as indicating sufficient immunity in the population to prevent an epidemic, despite the increase in measles cases. analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform public health strategies by highlighting the importance of maintaining high vaccination coverage and strengthening surveillance systems to detect and respond to measles outbreaks effectively.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on statistical data from surveillance systems, which may be subject to underreporting or delays. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on reported cases and does not include direct clinical or biological data from individual patients.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the resurgence of measles in Japan following the lifting of border control measures for COVID-19 in 2023. It reports a significant increase in measles cases from 28 in 2023 to 265 in 2025, with a majority of cases classified as modified measles. The study highlights that 60% of cases were suspected to be domestically acquired, while 66 cases were linked to overseas travel. Despite a high proportion of measles antibody titers ≥2 (96.1%), vaccination coverage for both routine doses remained below the 95% target. The findings emphasize the need for improved vaccination rates and enhanced surveillance systems to prevent further outbreaks. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on reported cases and surveillance data, with limitations in direct clinical or biological analysis.

full_text: The United States has lost its measles elimination status – an international designation reflecting an absence of local measles transmission for at least 12 months – a public health achievement held since 2000. A commission of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional office of the World Health Organization that oversees the Americas, reached that conclusion in November 2026, with a formal announcement expected Nov. 17. Canada lost its measles elimination status in 2025, as did the United Kingdom and other countries in Europe and central Asia in early 2026. These losses of status are no mystery. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases and still circulates in much of the world. What keeps the disease in check is herd immunity – when a high enough percentage of the population is vaccinated to break the chains of transmission. For measles, that’s at least 95%. But in 2025-26, only 92% of kindergartners in the U.S. received the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine. I’m an epidemiologist who studies misinformation in the same way others study smoking or air pollution: as an exposure that makes populations sick. For years I’ve watched vaccine misinformation help erode the coverage that kept measles from spreading. An effective vaccine A measles vaccine has existed in the U.S. since 1963. The combined MMR vaccine followed in 1971; two doses are about 97% effective. A federal program created in 1993 made it free for eligible children. After widespread vaccination efforts, reported cases dropped more than 99%, and by 2000 measles was declared eliminated. But due to the success of the MMR vaccine, within a generation most parents and many doctors had never even seen a measles case. The experts who certified elimination in 2000 warned that maintaining elimination status would require sustained high rates of vaccination, fast outbreak response and strong surveillance. Drop any one of these conditions and imported cases would spread. So how does a country with a 97% effective vaccine lose measles elimination status? One obvious explanation: The vaccine worked so well that people forgot what the disease does. Before the vaccine, measles infected 3 million to 4 million Americans a year. Tens of thousands were hospitalized, and hundreds died. Parents didn’t need convincing. They had seen it. Even with most cases unreported, the official count in 1963 was nearly 400,000 cases. About 1 in 20 children who contract measles develop pneumonia. The virus can also erase part of the immune system’s memory, an effect called immune amnesia, leaving children open to infections they had already beaten. In rare cases, it causes a fatal brain disease, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, which appears years after apparent recovery. In 2025, a child in Los Angeles died of it. A surge of outbreaks – and deaths As of Nov. 12, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted 5,412 cases for 2026 – the highest number since 1991 – and 591 hospitalizations. Among children under 5, 1 in 6 have been hospitalized. Six deaths appear in the CDC’s 2026 count, which now relies on federal death certificate data. States, using a broader definition, report a total of 10 deaths: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin. Pennsylvania’s outbreak alone has produced 1,542 cases and 305 hospitalizations, by the state’s Nov. 13 count. Major outbreaks have also hit South Carolina, Utah and Arizona since the West Texas outbreak of early 2025, which was the start of the national surge of measles outbreaks. Utah’s outbreak, which began in June 2025, has gone well past the 12-month mark. That outbreak alone breaches the WHO’s definition of measles elimination and could have triggered the loss of elimination status. Fertile ground for misinformation When no one remembers the disease, the vaccine becomes the only thing left to fear. Misinformation feeds on that imbalance. Parents who had never seen measles had nothing vivid to weigh against claims of vaccine risk, so even discredited risks felt plausible. A 1998 paper fraudulently linking MMR to autism was retracted in 2010, and its author lost his medical license. But the damage was already done, and this myth persists to this day, even though studies that included millions of children have found no link. During the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine misinformation proliferated in echo chambers on social media. It is no surprise that the percentage of kindergartners who have received their MMR shots has fallen every year since the 2019-20 school year. In a 2025 KFF poll, parents who believed any false measles claim were more than twice as likely to have skipped or delayed vaccines. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the anti-vaccine movement has also used the banner of medical freedom to gain a larger, more mainstream audience. Federal policy fuels further confusion Now these arguments have found an audience in federal policy. On Aug. 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed an order calling for MMR to be split into three single-disease shots, which are not sold in the United States. There is no published evidence that separating MMR offers any benefit, and more doctor visits mean more chances for missed doses. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested in August that Pennsylvania’s first two measles-associated deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” State officials had investigated both. While questioning the vaccine and measles deaths, he has promoted vitamin A and nutrition as measles cures. The CDC classifies vitamin A as a supportive treatment, not a cure or vaccine substitute. Vaccination rates for the MMR vaccine among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% in 2019-20 to 92.4% in 2025-26. Exemptions from any required vaccine rose to a record 4.2%. Of this year’s cases, 96% were unvaccinated or of unknown status. The 92.4% kindergarten vaccination rate leaves about 280,000 kindergartners without documented MMR. Among states, Idaho has the lowest MMR rate with 75.2% among Idaho kindergartners, while some counties and communities there and elsewhere have even lower rates. Adult immunity also has gaps: Adults are 41% of this year’s cases, and 15% of them were hospitalized. Many who were vaccinated before 1989, when a second MMR dose was added, got only one. Roadblocks to recovery Regaining elimination status means the U.S experiencing at least 12 months without continuous transmission. That will require the same factors that led to the U.S. earning that status in 2000: stronger surveillance, speedy outbreak response and increased vaccination rates. But it will also require federal health leadership that is focused on bringing those things about. The Department of Health and Human Services blames current vaccination gaps on missed pediatrician appointments during the COVID-19 pandemic. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said that the agency would not make any changes in measles response efforts in light of losing elimination status. Additionally, orders like August’s about the MMR vaccine, and revisions to long-standing vaccine recommendations, are weakening vaccination efforts. Also, on top of a chronically underfunded public health infrastructure , many career public health scientists lost their jobs in 2025. The surveillance capacity that made elimination possible has been substantially weakened. So what does this mean for Americans? The loss of measles elimination status in the U.S. does not change the fact that the vaccine is safe and effective – and it is now more important than ever.

Even with most cases unreported, the official count in 1963 was nearly 400,000 cases. States, using a broader definition, report a total of 10 deaths: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin. In 2025, a child in Los Angeles died of it. earning that status in 2000: stronger surveillance, speedy outbreak response and increased vaccination rates. Also, on top of a chronically underfunded public health infrastructure , many career public health scientists lost their jobs in 2025. Among states, Idaho has the lowest MMR rate with 75.2% among Idaho kindergartners, while some counties and communities there and elsewhere have even lower rates.

title: Daily briefing: Can you spot the ‘tortured phrases’?

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here. Voyager 1 is one light-day from Earth Today, as of 10:16 GMT, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has journeyed one light-day, or 25.9 billion kilometres, from Earth — farther than any human-made object has gone before. At this distance, signals from Earth’s surface travelling at light speed will take a full 24 hours to reach the craft. The trailblazing probe is expected to lose communications with Earth in 2029, when its plutonium power finally dies. But that time might not signal the end of Voyager 1’s contributions — the craft carries a golden record engraved with sights and sounds from Earth, an interspecies message for any aliens who might encounter it as it continues its journey. Alzheimer’s headset flops in critical trial A device that stimulates the brain with flickering light and rhythmic clicking sounds has failed to slow memory loss in people with Alzheimer’s disease. The Spectris AD headset is designed to induce brain activity called gamma waves, which have been linked to increased attention and memory. The results of a long-anticipated clinical trial showed that participants who used the device did not show robust improvements in their cognitive function after a year of treatment compared with those assigned to a sham treatment. The results were reported at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease meeting on 16 November. US loses measles elimination status The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has announced that the United States has lost its measles elimination status amid an outbreak that’s caused more than 5,700 infections and 10 deaths this year. The US had eliminated measles in 2000 after an intensive vaccination campaign. But declining vaccination rates in the past few years have left pockets of the population vulnerable to infection. “We’ve taken an enormous step back in public health,” says virologist Paul Offit. Measles has also been re-established in Mexico and Bolivia, PAHO announced. Features & opinion At-home microbiome tests Consumer tests that promise to reveal the full range of microbes living in your gut are taking off — but their results can vary widely. “This is an industry that’s running wild,” says genomicist Jacques Ravel, who co-authored a study that tested several providers. With regard to testing methods, he says, “there’s no standard”. But it’s hard to set those standards, writes journalist Amber Dance, who sent off her own stool to investigate the field. Part of the problem is that “there is no known ‘ground truth’ for a natural microbial sample”, she says. Quiz: can you spot a tortured phrase? Amid the tedium of investigating potentially fraudulent papers, “there is some light relief, thanks to some hilarious phrases used by authors seeking to avoid detection by plagiarism checkers”, writes research-integrity sleuth Dorothy Bishop. Bishop and Nature’s careers team have compiled a quiz to test your ability to match ‘tortured phrases’ — those that replace common words with synonyms in an attempt to skirt past plagiarism-detection software — with their original text. Take the Tortured Phrases Quiz The lost history of ‘Aquaterra’ From the Bering Strait to Doggerland, much of human history occurred in places that are now underwater, covered by the sea-level rise that occurs after ice ages. Geographer Jerome Dobson has dubbed this drowned land ‘Aquaterra’. It’s the site of many discoveries — such as Blinkerwall in the Baltic Sea, one of Europe’s oldest and largest Stone Age structures — and possibly many more to come. Voyager 1 is one light-day from Earth Today, as of 10:16 GMT, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has journeyed one light-day, or 25.9 billion kilometres, from Earth — farther than any human-made object has gone before. At this distance, signals from Earth’s surface travelling at light speed will take a full 24 hours to reach the craft. The trailblazing probe is expected to lose communications with Earth in 2029, when its plutonium power finally dies. But that time might not signal the end of Voyager 1’s contributions — the craft carries a golden record engraved with sights and sounds from Earth, an interspecies message for any aliens who might encounter it as it continues its journey. Alzheimer’s headset flops in critical trial A device that stimulates the brain with flickering light and rhythmic clicking sounds has failed to slow memory loss in people with Alzheimer’s disease. The Spectris AD headset is designed to induce brain activity called gamma waves, which have been linked to increased attention and memory. The results of a long-anticipated clinical trial showed that participants who used the device did not show robust improvements in their cognitive function after a year of treatment compared with those assigned to a sham treatment. The results were reported at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease meeting on 16 November. US loses measles elimination status The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has announced that the United States has lost its measles elimination status amid an outbreak that’s caused more than 5,700 infections and 10 deaths this year. The US had eliminated measles in 2000 after an intensive vaccination campaign. But declining vaccination rates in the past few years have left pockets of the population vulnerable to infection. “We’ve taken an enormous step back in public health,” says virologist Paul Offit. Measles has also been re-established in Mexico and Bolivia, PAHO announced. Part of the problem is that “there is no known ‘ground truth’ for a natural microbial sample”, she says. Quiz: can you spot a tortured phrase?
